utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Kupreskic, I'd like you to tell us about your relations with your brother Zoran. Throughout the trial, I see you sitting next to one another, and I had the feeling that you were inseparable. It might be a wrong impression, given the circumstances of the trial, but could you tell us how your relations were with your brother then and how they have developed since?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran, my brother, is five years older than I am, so we are not peers. We are not of the same age. By being brothers, we're more than brothers, because it was this folklore which brought us together. First we danced together there, and after that, Zoran led that company and I managed the rehearsals. So I can say that apart from being brothers, there was also this additional fun that we had together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us talk about this period going from the end of 1992 to April 1993. Did you then, you and your brother, meet every day, be it at his house or at your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't say that we met every day, but our folklore rehearsals took place three or four times a week so that we would go together to those rehearsals, come back from the rehearsals together, and I was with Zoran. Whenever I met all my other friends from the folklore company, he was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So besides the rehearsals of the folklore group, you had brotherly relations but you were not always together; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran was employed by the SPS company, and I worked for the wholesale unit of Sutre, and, of course, during that period of time, we were completely separated. Whether we would have coffee together every evening, whether he came to my place or I to his, whether it was every evening, every second evening, every fifth evening, I really can't say, but, of course, the working hours that I spent at my company and the hours that he spent working at his company were the times when we were not together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would it be accurate or inaccurate to say that Zoran, since he was the elder brother, had some authority over you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, we were already grown up, so Zoran had his own family and I had my own family. All I could do was obey Zoran in some -- accept some good suggestions that he would have for me. But whether he had any authority over me, I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, today is the 102nd day of these trial proceedings. We talked at length about what happened in Ahmici on the 16th of April. I would like you to tell us now how you feel about these dramatic events, how you look at the events and how you analyse them.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Today, I can say that a terrible crime happened in Ahmici, and it must be punished, but I always wonder, "What am I doing here? Why am I associated to this crime?" I did nothing bad. All I could do that day, it was beyond me, beyond my powers, and I'm so sorry, as I've said. I've shed rivers of tears for my friend. I would have been the happiest man on earth had he survived because in addition to being friends, we also had common interests. Nobody can replace that man for me. I miss him both as a friend and as a man who worked together with me, who made money together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to remind you of the fact that Fahrudin is not the only victim who fell on that day and that the event is relevant enough for you to think about what had happened, besides what happened to you personally.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I agree with you that Fahrudin was not the only victim. There were countless victims down there. I did say that a horrendous crime was committed there. People died brutally, and I'm sorry. I very much regret all that happened, but I always keep asking myself, "What am I doing here?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, you told us that you did your military service in 1984 within the JNA. Could you tell us what distinctions or qualifications you obtained during the military service or what kind of training you received?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the army, I was with the military band of the former Yugoslav People's Army, and most of my military service I spent with the military band, with another five men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So apart from this musical activity, did you not receive any proper military training?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: While doing my military service, I was trained as an infantry man. The training lasted for four months, although I was somewhat in a privileged position because of the band.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So let's leave the music aside for a moment. I'm asking you whether you received military training during your military service and, more specifically, whether you learned how to use weapons. Could you give me a specific answer to this?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that I completed a four-month training, as any other soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, you then learned how to use firearms. You learned to use the weapons that were then used in the former Yugoslav army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Kupreskic, that as of August 1992, you started working for the Sutre company. I understood that you first worked in Grabovi and then in Vitez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is true that I first worked, that is, that I got a job with this wholesale unit which was in Ahmici, and on the eve of the conflict, right before the conflict, I moved to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us during what period you worked at the Sutre shop in Grabovi and when you worked in the Vitez shop?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that as of August 1992, and the wholesale in Ahmici, I worked there until -- well, I cannot tell you exactly, but it was about ten days, whether it was the 6th or the 7th or the 8th of April, 1993 when I moved to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Most of your time that you spent in the Sutre company until April 1993, you spent in the shop that was in Vitez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Between the 6th or the 7th, whenever it was when I went there, at that time, I would go to work in the shop in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that time, the Sutre shop was operational. It was open, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The whole Sutre wholesale worked, yes. There was a man who used to work with me. There was another man, and while I was with the wholesale unit, he worked together with me, and when I moved to the retail unit in Vitez, that man stayed behind and took over all the wholesale business.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understood. The only thing I still have to ask you in this regard is to know who that other person was who kept running the Sutre shop.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was Ivica Covic. He is Vlatko Kupreskic's in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Throughout that period, is it true to say that your boss, your employer, the most direct employer, was Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout the time I worked there, during that particular period of time and after the war, Ivica was the boss all the time. Ivica was the one who gave me the job, and I accounted to Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, say, if Ivica was to go to Germany or when he did his trips to Croatia, did somebody replace him?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The jobs, the work that Ivica did, there was hardly anyone who could replace him fully, I mean, in everything that he did. Some of this business, if he was away, well, some of it I did, if it came to paperwork and things like that. But there was nobody to take his place when he was away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you would go from your home to your workplace in Vitez, and how would you come back? Were you being driven by somebody or would you go by bus or some other means of public transport?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a rule, and I'm referring to about ten days or so before the conflict, as a rule, and that is why I said that I went to this coffee shop Set, Zdravko Vrebac's coffee shop, because that is where we met as musicians, and there was always somebody who would give me a lift, somebody who was going in that direction, and that was usually how I travelled back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's say, for instance, in the morning, when you would leave your house to go to work, how did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If Ivica was at home, then I would go by his car. We went together. When Ivica was away, there was a bus or a van between Nadioci, Vitez, and further on, that was its usual route, and so I would commute that way. At times, I would go down to the road and lift my finger, and somebody would give me a ride. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that at that time you used to live in the same house as your parents did. Was it your house or did the house belong to your parents?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is my father's house, and I have nothing to do with that house to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a phone in the house?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did your father have a car in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you stated that you were on very good terms with a lot of Muslims who lived either in Ahmici or in Vitez but that basically none of them were willing to testify in this trial because they were under pressure or maybe they received threats. Could you tell us whether those witnesses you have in mind are character witnesses who might have been in a position to tell the Court about your personality, your character, or whether they were fact witnesses who might have said, for instance, that you were not in the house of which the Prosecution states that you were in? Do you see what I mean? Are they character witnesses or fact witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I spoke about them, I had in mind three or four friends of mine who know me exceptionally well and could not testify as to the facts because those people were not there at the time. They could only testify as to my character, what kind of man was I, what I was and whether I was capable of doing that, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, none of the fact witnesses were prevented from testifying or from coming here to support you in your defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not in touch with any of the witnesses. I mentioned here three or four, and to them, through my defence lawyers, my defence lawyers were in touch with them, and those are the witnesses that I mentioned a little while ago and in what respect I mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Mentioning these character witnesses who might have received pressures or be under pressure or have received threats not to be Defence witnesses, could you tell us who might have exerted pressure on them, who might have threatened them, what was the form of these threats, and why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say who threatened them. Yesterday, when I said that it was one of the conclusions, because the first time they talked to them, they were ready to do anything, to come here even. The second time, it was less so, and I talked about a videolink or a deposition. Then again, the next time, even less so. So that is why I conjectured, I inferred that there must have been some threats, because I know those people well and I'm quite positive that they would have come, had it not been for those threats. But again, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I've thought about that. Since you have not been able to say who might have been at the origin of threats or pressures, do you have any idea as to why they might have done that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said I did not know who threatened them, those were only assumptions, and I cannot really say who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One last question on this. Witness, I'm not asking you to give us the first and last names of those who may have exerted pressures or threats, since you say you don't know. I'm only asking you whether you have any idea as to why such pressures were expressed so that the witnesses would not testify, not who by but why? If you don't know, you don't know. Still, if you have some ideas, please convey them to us.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only repeat that specifically I do not know. I only assume because I know those people, who they are and what they are, they would have come had somebody not prevailed upon them or threatened them, and I know them because these people live in that environment and they receive help from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let's move on to something else because you think that pressures might have been exerted on the witnesses but you don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown, once more, D112, one of the very latest ones this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This is a demobilisation certificate. The second sentence, there's a first paragraph and a second sentence which reads as follows: "The named person is to be in RR in his basic unit." What does this sentence mean, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My guess is that this is a wartime assignment. That is the unit that I was with at the defence line during that period of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, with all due respect, I'd like to show you that this sentence applies to the future, to the period following the 31st of May, 1994. It doesn't state in which unit or work schedule you found yourself during the war. This sentence says that following demobilisation, you are supposed to stay in RR, in that position qualified as being RR. Am I wrong? This sentence turns to the future, not to the past, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're quite right, and it says that the named person will still be assigned to his basic unit, and that is the one that I spent my time with during the war. So this should be my unit, and I would be still assigned to that particular unit in the future too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Given this specification, could you tell us what your status was with respect to the HVO at the time of your demobilisation? In other words, did you then become again a reserve person?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. After I was demobilised and after I returned all the gear, I was at the disposal of the defence office, just as I was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Prior to the war and after the demobilisation, you were a reservist; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to use the register again, it's been used a lot before, unless you want to see it again, but some mentions are made with regard to you. Are those entries accurate or inaccurate, given what you've just said? I remind you that in the register, it is stated that you are a "P" category, a reservist, from April 1992 until 1996. So that doesn't seem to be inaccurate, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is not correct because I believe that between the 18th of April, I think I was mobilised then until, as it says here, the 31st of May. So it was the period of time when I was mobilised. Before that, I was with the reserve, and after that, after the 31st of May, I was a reservist again, and this is what I am to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you explain to us what a reservist had in terms of work duties? Could you be as specific as possible when it comes to your assignments?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please clarify, what period of time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Just in general terms, a person who was part of the Croatian community who was then a reserve person in Central Bosnia, what would such a person have in terms of duties in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was a reservist, and I was on the defence office list. So if the defence office would call me up, send me a summons or something, they could do it either to enter some new data about me or to mobilise me or for any other reason. I was registered with the defence office on that list, and I did my usual work at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you under the obligation to train, to do some training, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I myself, I personally never attended -- never went to any drill. Whether it was in 1985 or '86, after I did my military service, I did get a summons to report to the Defence office and I was supposed to go to a military drill, but it coincided in time with my departure to Germany because we had a concert there, so that I went there, explained it to them, and I was relieved of that drill and they allowed me to go to Germany. That was the only time when I was summoned to attend to take part in a drill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you had obtained an M-48 gun at some point in time. Could you tell us when you obtained that weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't tell you the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Just give us the period, then.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was December, when those refugees from Turbe, Didaks, came to Ivica's brother's houses, Josip, and it was about then that Zdravko Didak gave me that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why did this refugee give you this M-48 gun?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those people were on defence lines facing the Serbs, they came from Turbe, and they were quite well supplied with weapons. They had brought their family to that part of the village. They knew that we kept guard, that we had those village guards. And in my house, there was no weapon of any kind and he had this rifle, and he simply gave it to me, and also to protect his family, because they were living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know Nenad Santic, but I don't know what you're referring to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like you to tell us about the role or the part played in that village at that time by Nenad Santic. I want to ask you if you can tell us what the role Nenad Santic played there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he was in the HDZ, that he was one of the first there, but what his exact role was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have any relations with him? Were you in touch with him? Did you have contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had no personal contacts with Nenad Santic. If I saw him, I would greet him, just like anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you say that at that time in Ahmici, Santici, Pirici, Nenad Santic was a man of authority, of some authority and an influential man, a prominent person?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not perceive him as such. To me, he did not represent anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Some time ago, we spoke about a witness who saw you in a uniform, and other witnesses who testified here, and you must remember them, also saw you in a uniform, in a camouflage uniform, and that was in the period which preceded April 1993. I mean particularly Witness S, and that is page 2.946 of the transcript, and I also have in mind Witness Z, who testified here on the 5th of October, '98, who said that shortly after the events of October '92, he saw you stand guard near the roadblock which was set up near Ahmici, and we often refer to that roadblock. So did you stand guard at that particular roadblock in the company of other Croats, as this witness says?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If this is the witness whom I am thinking of and who was here, he was together with me at that point, and that refers to the meeting on Ivica's terrace at his house, and we were the first who showed up at that point. He appeared with me, and I think that it was [redacted], and I think that the four of us were all there together first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I was not asking you to give us any names, but they do not correspond to those names that I have before my eyes. Perhaps we could go into private session because of those names, please. Witness, will you please not read out the names, not read out their names. So you stood guard at this roadblock with those persons, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you confirm what this person says, that Ivica Kupreskic and Vinko Vidovic were also at the same place where you were?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vinko Vidovic could have been there, because Vinko Vidovic's house was about 50 metres from there, from the intersection of that road. But I'm repeating that Ivica, myself and the name I just mentioned were all there at that location for the first time. Vinko could have been there, but at that point he was not there as a guard. I know that some other people would come by and they would stop by there and be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember that this witness also said, according to the transcript, that the three of you, that is, you, Mirjan Kupreskic, Ivica Kupreskic and Vinko Vidovic, mounted guard at that particular checkpoint in camouflage uniforms and also that you had automatic rifles with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that sometimes I had Zoran's jacket, and it is possible that on that day I was wearing that jacket. As far as the rifles are concerned, Ivica by that time already had the automatic rifle and that other automatic rifle that was around at that time, so that may have been there at that checkpoint, at that barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could it be possible that you were the one who carried such an automatic rifle, since you were mounting guard there and that you had an automatic rifle there, an AK-47?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said, we had one automatic rifle which belonged to Miroslav Pudze, and there was this hunting rifle which belonged to Mirko Sakic. Immediately after the conflict, Ivica also bought himself an automatic rifle. Ivica Sakic bought himself an automatic rifle. I don't know which one I had on me, but there were two automatic rifles at that checkpoint, and those were left behind for the next shift who arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So to make it all quite clear, you do not exclude the possibility of mounting guard at that particular checkpoint and having with you an automatic rifle; it is a possibility, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said I can confirm that I was on that checkpoint and I had an automatic rifle. I explained which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On other occasions, did you have in your hands a similar type of automatic rifle, on different occasions and in different places?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During these patrols, sometimes I would have this automatic rifle on me, sometimes I would carry the hunting rifle. It depends. I could have been using both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That automatic rifle, it is an AK-47; is that what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was an automatic rifle. I'm not sure whether it was that particular model.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, but don't you know what an AK-47 is?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I guess I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So that automatic rifle that you had, was that an AK-47?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, or you could name it Kalashnikov, or sometimes it was also nicknamed Gypsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we finally know what it was. Now, let us talk for a while about another witness. Are we still in -- no, I shall not mention the name because we're in open session. I'm referring to a young man who testified here, who saw you, who stated that he had seen you that 16th of April, 1993, in the house of Jozo Livancic. I won't mention his name, but I presume you know who it is. It is Witness C. Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [redacted] 10 [redacted] 11 [redacted] 12 [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. My mistake. Please receive my apologies, but I don't think that the witness will be confused about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So, Witness, do you want me to show you the name of that person, our Witness C? You know who it is about. I wonder, on what terms were you with that person, if you were on any terms, prior to the 16th of April, 1993? Did you know that person?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean the person or the person in whose house we were?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Just a moment. I mean the witness who testified here.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a child. I may have met this child when going to Vitez, he may have been riding his bike, but I had no particular relations with him because we were far apart in age. At that time, he was a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But did you at least know him if you saw him? Could you say, "Yes, I know that particular person. He lives in Ahmici and his house is in that part of Ahmici"? I mean would you know who the talk was about?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right now, I know very well who it was, but at that time he was still a child. Whether I would have been able to recognise him among other children, I'm not sure. I could have been mistaken. But I knew his parents, because we knew the parents very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question. I was going to ask you if you had any particular relations with that family, and I mean the parents of that young man, and I also mean the elder sister of that young man. You are telling me that your parents and their parents exchanged visits, paid calls, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My parents had good relations with his parents, and I knew his sister. I would greet her, and as well as other neighbours and family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you are not disputing that you knew this young man?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether this young man knew me, but I said how I knew them, so the boy may have known me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that time between your two families, that is, the family of that boy and your family and your brother's family, were there any disagreements with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were never any disputes or any problems between those two families.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You heard the testimony of this young boy. What did you think of that? Could you give us some explanation?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I only know that this boy did not tell the truth here. I don't know whether he was confused. I don't know his motives. I had no reasons, I had no strength, I had no courage at that time to be in a place where he said he saw me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us if you had any particular contact, or regular, or episodic contact with Jozo Alilovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Personally, I never went to Jozo Alilovic, to his house, that means, nor did I have any contacts with Jozo Alilovic. I knew this man as a church person, as a person who collects the alms, the contributions in the church, but I personally never knew him and had any dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you say the same of your brother Zoran?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that Zoran had a similar situation as I did with regard to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did Jozo Alilovic visit your parents in the house in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This could have happened, because this Jozo had a small tractor, and sometimes when we worked in the fields, he would come to just work the field. Those would be the only occasions when he would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But do you remember that? Do you have a recollection of that? You're saying it could happen or it happened, but do you remember that? Do you have a recollection of it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Jozo Alilovic did come several times and did what I just described with his tractor at my parents' field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that on the 16th of April, in the morning, your friend Zoran woke you up. Do you have any idea as to what time that was? At what time did your friend Zoran wake you up?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was around 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember looking at a watch or a clock or something?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had a clock in my house, and I looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When Zoran came to warn you, to rouse you, was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran was dressed. He had that camouflage uniform on already by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When Zoran warned you and told you to get ready, did he tell you what he was about to do?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran told me to get ready because there was information that Mujahedin were to attack from Barin Gaj. I asked him, "Where did you get this information," and he said that Dragan had come by and told him so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did Zoran tell you where you should go, where your family should take shelter? Did he tell you what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran did not tell me where we were going. We were going to go to the shelter, and as we did this several times before, it was a routine of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you went out with your family, could you tell, even approximately, what time was it then?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how long it took for us to get ready and to do this with my mother-in-law, but it was definitely before 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could one think that, as you came out of the house, you looked around a little bit, perhaps in the direction of Muslim houses, would it be absurd to think that you thought that everything was calm, that everybody was asleep in that direction, that you could see no lights and that you heard no sound?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Listen, at that moment, I had no time, nor did I look around my house. I was just looking to leave as soon as possible and to reach the shelter, and I described who I had to take care of and take with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to show us on the aerial photograph Barin Gaj, at least in which direction it is from which you think that attack might have come? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Barin Gaj would be somewhere around here (indicating) or this area here. So this is Pirici, this is just above Pirici, and this is where our houses were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can take your seat again. Now, you showed us the direction in which Barin Gaj is. You believed that a Mujahedin attack might come from there, and you showed us the approximate direction, of course, bearing in mind that this map is turned upside down, but you more or less pointed northward, didn't you, in the direction of north?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you explain to me then, as you had to flee as quickly as possible, you told me that you were in a great hurry, that you were pressed for time. Wouldn't it have been quicker to go down that road, to take that route, that is, the main road, to get to Rovna? Wouldn't it have been simpler and quicker to do it by car and safer, after all, for your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, we needed about half an hour to get all the way up to Rovna, and as far as the Vrebac shelter is concerned, we need not more than 10 to 15 minutes. The closest we had was the Vrebac shelter, and the shortest route there was the path we took to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that your mother-in-law was crippled or, rather, that she walked with difficulty, that she needed a stick, you told us that your son Marko was ill, and you, therefore, told us that you put her in a wheelbarrow in order to push her to Vrebac's shelter. But in view of all these problems, wouldn't it have been more logical and simpler and safer, above all, to have somebody help you who had a car, your brother or perhaps Vlatko Kupreskic, and to take you either to Rovna or in the direction of Busovaca or Vitez? It is that kind of behaviour that we don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have spent more time if somebody had come in a car while we were packing and then came around, went to the main road, then around and around through the -- down the main road. So using this path, it was much faster than by using a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You're saying that it was quicker to push the wheelbarrow with your mother-in-law down to the depression and to Vrebac' shelter than to take a car?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The route you needed to take, if you were to use the car, you would have had to go to the main road, then the main road to Pican's coffee bar, and then around. So you would have to go like this, like this, and like that, whereas I went over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This morning, you told us it was cold, that there was drizzle also, and yet I'd like you to explain to us one thing: We have a situation which is a high alert, a dangerous situation, and a number of Croat families which are either in Grabovi or Ahmici and which are forced to look for shelter as quickly as possible, some of them moving in the direction of Zume, some to Radak's bridge in the direction of Rovna, and others hiding in the woods. Yet the majority of these families, if not all of them, have a car, and yet nobody, and you will correct me if I am wrong, nobody uses his car.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone used their car, and I don't know who you're referring to. I know that I did not use it. I know that my brother and my parents did not use the car. I described how we went there and that we did not use the car. I don't know whether anybody else did use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But did you hear anyone say, I mean, any Croat and resident of Ahmici say that that morning, the 16th of April, he fled by using his car?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not hear about it. Perhaps some of Drago Josipovic's people, they may have used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What happened to your father? I don't think that you mentioned him during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean? When did something happen to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Just tell us whether he came along with you or stayed in the house, because you didn't talk of your father at all during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Father went together with mother and in this group where my family and where Zoran's family was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wanted to know. Earlier on, you mentioned a group of Croatian soldiers you saw as you were going to the shelter, answering a question by Mrs. Glumac who was asking you how you understood, how you knew that these were Croatian soldiers. You said that they were Croatian because there, where they were, there were only Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the part where we encountered them, we call that area Pudzine Kuce, the Pudza houses, all of them are Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So since there are soldiers in that Croatian neighbourhood, you think that inevitably they are Croatian soldiers; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say that they were inevitably Croat soldiers, but if they were any other soldiers, you could have heard shooting or something would have happened, but nothing did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did those soldiers make the same impression on you as on your brother Zoran? Were you stricken with fear or terror when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was afraid. I said that they looked like commandos, and until then, I had seen such soldiers only in the movies. Of course, this instilled great fear in us, especially in the situation that I was in. I explained that I was with my child, with my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you sure that they had white belts and holsters?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sure that I saw white belts and holsters. They were white too. Whether they all had them, that, I don't know, but I'm sure that I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking you this question, which is not very relevant, is just that I'm somewhat surprised that a soldier should have a black painted face and would have a white belt if he goes to fight. But I move on to another question. If you were frightened by the soldiers, it was not because there was a situation of danger because of them, if you were afraid of them, it was because you thought of what they might be able to do in the village. Is that why you were frightened?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not know whether they would do anything and what these soldiers' intentions were. I was only terrified by the way they looked, these soldiers. It was so unusual, in terms of those days and those events, that such people would appear at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You followed a path to go to the shelter going through the depression. We saw this in photographs which were admitted earlier on this morning. Now, is that the most straight, direct, and fastest way, if you're walking, of course, to go from the group of Kupreskic houses to Zume?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From our houses to Zume, that is the closest possible path. That is a shortcut. There is no shorter way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So there is no other path or way than that one. Could it be said that apart from the times when you went to visit your family, you and your friends were on that path at some place, at some location on that path?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which path you are referring to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm thinking of this path we saw in the photographs, of which you have just said that this was the closest, the most natural way to go from your houses to Zume or from Zume to your houses.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The question was whether we were on that path, right, during that morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During the day of the 16th of April, 1993. Because you told us that you found yourselves, you were in the depression, that you spent most of the time that day in the depression. Were you on that path then that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that we spent most of the time in the upper part of the depression near that path that we're talking about, the one that leads from our houses. From time to time, we would venture along that path, 10 or 15 metres, and then we would return due to detonations or bullets that were flying through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It would be logical to think that anyone going that way, going from Zume to the Kupreskic houses, had to be seen by you and your friends.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not the way it was. That is a path that leads from our houses to Zume, but then you also have a road that goes down below Dragan Vidovic's house. That's a big road that you can take a car on, and then you can go to Zume and link up at the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't think that we understand each other. We seem to be talking at cross-purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for insisting on this because I think this is relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Beforehand, I was asking you whether you could tell us, that path that we saw in the photographs, is that the most natural, the most direct way, the fastest way to go through the depression going from the Sakic's houses and the Kupreskic's. Going through that depression, using that path, is that the fastest way to go, if you use that path?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I repeat: Only to our houses, it is the fastest way to get to our houses, the Kupreskic houses, my house, my brother's house, Ivica's house, and Ivica's brother's houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I think I have to ask you this question: At any point in time on that day, do you remember seeing Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, I did not see Vlatko Kupreskic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Didn't you worry about the fact that he was not together with you in the depression?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know where Vlatko was, and to tell you the truth, I never thought of him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that you were there on the rim or on the edge, on the eastern edge of the depression close to the Kupreskic houses, you were there from a vantage point to observe things, but what could you see at that time? What was your field of vision from there where you were?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the area that we were in, we could see towards Ivo Kupreskic's house, towards uncle's house, and we could see the field, the empty field that went from that house to the road. We could see that area completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So what were you able to see during that day in that clearing that you've just mentioned? What did you see on that day from there?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the area that I mentioned just now, I could not see a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: From that location where you were, from that observation point, you couldn't observe anything; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see anyone, but I did see that clearing, the clearing that led to the road. But if you're talking about a person, I did not see any person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Don't misunderstand me. I'm just trying to understand what happened. You are telling us that there were bullets everywhere, flying everywhere, that something was happening in that village. Houses were on fire. You didn't know which houses. You were there in order to look, and still you couldn't see anything. I'm just trying to say, did that happen all through the day and the night and then another day? Was that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that during those first three hours, while there was intense shooting, we did not know what was going on, whose houses were on fire. We just saw a lot of smoke, thick smoke from the direction of our houses and from the lower part of Ahmici. That's when we saw this thick smoke. At that point in time, we did not know which houses were in question. We just knew that there was shooting and that there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So this regards the first three hours, but what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After that, when we went to the shelter, when I received this terrible piece of news about my friend, as we passed to the shelter, we saw that there were houses that were burning in the area of Zume as well. We found out about my friend's death. When we were in the shelter and when we were going back, Zoran said that there were other persons who were dead too in this part down below, so we already knew that. As we were going back to the depression and when we saw Ivica, I asked Ivica, I said, "Have our houses burned down?" And Ivica said, "No, the houses are intact, but all the houses around our houses are burning," so that is yet another piece of information that we received. During the course of the day, until the evening and in the evening hours and the night hours, when there was this strong detonation around the mosque, we saw that the minaret was no longer there, and then we started realising what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that that morning or that day when you were in the depression, there were bullets flying over your head. I think this is the phrase you used in your examination-in-chief. Did you use this metaphor just to say that there was shooting or did you have the feeling that the shooting was directed at you, the bullets were flying above your heads? Do you know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I shall try to answer, if I understood you correctly. I think I did. When we were in this depression, we did not feel any bullets above our heads because we were in a hole, so to speak, but when we were trying to get out to this road or, rather, this path, at that point in time, the bullets were flying through the forest, and they could be felt on the trees and above the trees, and that is why we had to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you feel safe in the depression?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In those moments, no one felt safe anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Still, if you'd been in a shelter with a concrete slab above you, you might have felt safer.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Under such circumstances, when there was such a lot of shooting, was I supposed to be sitting next to my child in a shelter and was somebody supposed to come up and kill me and my child? Would I have been such an idiot to stay there with my child rather than stand in front of this shelter and try to save whatever could be saved?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Earlier on, you said that Satko Vidovic was the one who told you that your friend Fahran had died. Do you know how Satko Vidovic learned of Fahran's death, who by?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that his name is Anto Vidovic and his nickname was Satko. When he told me about this, I asked him whether this information was for sure, and he said that he heard about this from someone from the lower part of Zume and that the original information came from Fahran's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So somebody must have moved from the lower part of Ahmici to go to Zume in order to convey, among other things, this piece of information; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know who came from where. I'm just telling you how this was conveyed to me. He said that from the lower part of Zume, somebody had told him, and that the information actually came from Fahrudin's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember even approximately at what time you learned of his death?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact hour, but I link this to the first lull in the intensive shooting. So if this was 2.00 or 3.00, then the first time we went to the shelter could have been 9.00 or 9.30. That is the only thing I can say, quite approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you knew that Fahran was not armed?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I socialised with my friend Fahrudin, I knew that his rifle had been taken away from him. That I knew. He told me that. I also know that he had a small pistol. I don't know what kind of ammunition this was exactly. I know because at the time that we played in Turbe, when the Serbs started shelling Turbe, sometimes he would carry this pistol with him because it would give us a feeling of security or safety of sorts, so I knew that he had this small pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you learned that your friend Fahran had died, did you think that he was possibly a fighter on that day, on the 16th of April in Ahmici, and that he possibly died in combat; did you think that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not have thought that Fahrudin was a combatant, because I knew Fahrudin very well, and as far as I know, he was not attached to the army. I don't know whether he stood guard with the others. The first thought that crossed my mind was that it was a shell or a bullet, because under such circumstances, I could have lost my life too. That is the first thought that crossed my mind before I knew what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So your first thought was that Fahran might have been killed by a stray bullet or by a shell that might have happened to have been dropped on his house; is that what you first thought, say, at 9.00, around 9.00, 9.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know whether he was killed at home or in front of his home. I didn't know where this had happened. But the first assumption was the one that I mentioned, that this was due to a shell or -- I didn't know, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You stated that you were really upset when you learned of his death. I do not doubt your feelings at all, but I would like to know whether you took any steps in order to make sure that Fahran's family would be safe. I'm thinking of his wife, of his children, who were then without a father, without any support. Did you do anything to make sure that they were safe in a shelter?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Believe me, I didn't know where his family was. I said that at that first moment when I found out about his death, I did not know the circumstances, I did not know the circumstances under which he had died. I was thinking about my own family. Only during the night and during the course of the next day, I learned a bit more, that it was quite different in respect of what I had thought originally when I received the news of his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So what did you do? What steps did you take in order to find out about the fate of his family when you learned what had actually happened, that is, in the evening or the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not know where they were. I thought that they got out. I didn't know where they were, whatever. On the 17th, in the evening, when my family went to Rovna, I did not know about them either. I only knew that they were in Rovna, but I did not go up there to Rovna to see them. Only on the next day, after it had dawned, I went to Rovna to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that in the afternoon of the 16th of April, there had been a lull in the shooting, that the shooting had abated when the UNPROFOR APCs had been in the village. Did you see the APCs from there where you were, did you see the armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We heard the sound of these carriers from the road when they were in the lower part and at the point when they were reaching the intersection by Veleprodaja, and we could see them passing through there. At that point, there was a lull in the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where were the APCs in the village when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only briefly by the intersection by Veleprodaja, the road that leads to Gornji Ahmici. I don't know where they were afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: From the location where you were, you had some vantage point over a section of that road; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only in those moments when we would go up the path, it is only then that we could see that part, and those were moments when there was no shooting or when the shooting would start again and when we would have to go back. So these were just attempts that we made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But on the 16th of April, on that road, for just a fraction of a second you saw the UNPROFOR APCs, but never did you see any other soldiers or civilians, for that matter; you didn't see anybody on that road. Is that what you said before?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In those moments, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that there was a lull towards the late afternoon on the 16th of April. You said that there was an explosion that brought the minaret down. But you also said, unless I interpreted what you said wrongly, and then you can correct me, but you also said that the fighting had started again later on. Did I misinterpret you or did I interpret you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean after the explosion around the mosque that I spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After this explosion that we heard around the mosque, there was no shooting whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So if that was so, why did you not leave the depression in order to go to your houses to see what had happened, to see how things were in Grabovi? You could have done that earlier on, for instance, when the UNPROFOR entered the village, because you said that there was then a lull in the fighting. I would like to understand why you didn't use this opportunity, the lull in the fighting, to go and see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's easy to talk now, from this point of view. Now I know, and we're talking from here, when the UNPROFOR vehicles were there, there was no shooting for an hour. But at that time, I did not know whether they would start shooting again within a minute or a second or whether there wouldn't be any shooting for two hours. Then, I did not know that at all. But now I know that there was no shooting for two hours or for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But you also added that the next day, on the 17th of April, the shooting had shifted to Upper Ahmici, and therefore in Lower Ahmici -- please correct me again if I'm wrong, but also in Grabovi, there was no fighting anymore, or nothing that looked like or sounded like shooting or firing or that could be understood as being a dangerous situation of fighting, and still you remained in the depression?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that the shooting had moved towards the upper area, that is to say, Grabovi too. We consider that part, Grabovi, to be pretty far away from our houses, but it was still near our houses, and an even greater danger for us was this part -- how shall I explain this? This part near Ivica's house, near our uncle's house and this new building that was built afterwards, that was not there at the time, that's that clearing, and it was very dangerous to cross that part in order to reach our houses. We knew that in a part there in Pirici, there was a machine gun that was either operating at that time or -- I don't know, but anyway it was very dangerous to cross that clearing then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you say that there was a machine gun that was operating in Pirici on that day, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say whether it was actually shooting on that day or not, but we knew that there was a machine gun in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But that machine gun would belong to whom? Who was it used by?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We knew that Naser -- no, not Naser. Zehir, Zehir Ahmici had this machine gun and he kept it, and he lived in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you hear that machine gun being fired on the 16th or the 17th? Did you see shooting coming from Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say that I heard it, that I could distinguish that amidst the terrible shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So there was this clearing between you and your houses. Did it possibly come under the fire of that machine gun?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say. I said that I did not see where it was actually being fired from, but that is one of the reasons why we were afraid to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So to sum it up, starting from the lull on the 16th and throughout that day, the night of the 16th to the 17th, to the 17th and the following night, you remained in the depression and did not move from it. That means that you didn't go to your houses to see what was happening there. So even if the shooting was more remote, you thought that you could still possibly be the target of something, of some weapon that might be located in Pirici; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that that was one of the reasons. That was not the one and only reason. There was a clearing. There was a danger for one's life from all sides, not only there. And, on the other hand, I was not really interested in the house anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: However, Ivica Kupreskic did move quite freely across that clearing, according to the testimony we heard here in court and which you heard yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not say that he moved freely, and how he happened to be there and how he remained, he's the only one who knows. Ivica had this wholesale business, he had a lot of goods, he had a house in which he had invested a lot. He's that kind of person. He liked money, he liked to live and work, and I can only assume that these were his reasons. And how he stayed up there, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the time has come for us to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I would like to say something. Your Honours, please, is it possible tomorrow for us to start the hearing earlier, or could we work until a later hour so that we could manage to hear the accused Vlatko Kupreskic during the course of this week? Namely, the interest of our defence is that the testimony of Vlatko Kupreskic should be completed entirely, not for us to start the questioning this week and then the cross-examination to be continued by the Prosecutor, I don't know, sometime in September. So I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to try to make a timetable which would make it possible for us to finish with the examination of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic this week. In addition, may I add that the Defence is going to complete its examination in chief during the course of one working day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina, I think your request is quite sensible, and I think you are right that we should finish by Friday. We can only suggest that we should sit tomorrow from 9.00 to 1.30, and on Friday from 9.00 to 1.00 and then from 2.30 to 5.30, if need be. But let us make enough effort to finish as soon as possible. In any case, I agree with you that the examination and cross-examination of Vlatko Kupreskic should finish by Friday. So we'll adjourn now until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of July, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
